📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations.
  • It has been revealed that however, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Significant Bang.
  • It has been revealed that the study was led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. Scientists theorized that these were early quasars, galaxies with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) powered by the "seeds" that would grow to become supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

It has been revealed that however, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Significant Bang. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars, "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, latest simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars.

It has been revealed that the study was led by Dr. Daniel Whalen from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation. His colleagues included researchers from United Arab Emirates University, the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the Institute for Astronomy and Royal Observatory at the University of Edinburgh, and the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA). The paper detailing their findings was published in the The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Sources indicate that the little red dots could represent galaxies in an evolutionary phase predating the luminous quasar phase. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/ISTA)/ETH Zurich/NAOJ.

In a recent development, previous attempts to explain the rapid formation, abundance, and spectral characteristics of LRDs all suffered from the same issue. While each explained some characteristics, none could account for everything the JWST revealed in its deep field surveys. Then came the DCBHs theory, which argues that SMBH seeds formed directly from massive clouds of cold gas. While this theory did fit Webb's observations nicely, it still faces numerous theoretical and environmental challenges.

For starters, the core premise of the DCBH theory is that a massive cloud of cold gas could collapse under its own gravity. However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. To prevent fragmentation, the gas cloud must remain hot, requiring a very specific amount of Lyman-Werner (LW) radiation from a synchronized star-forming galaxy in its vicinity to destroy the main coolant - i.e., molecular hydrogen (Hâ).

It has been revealed that this raises additional problems, including the self-shielding nature of molecular hydrogen. As a gas cloud becomes increasingly dense, its outer layers absorb the LW radiation, shielding the inner core. This means that the critical amount of radiation required to suppress cooling across the entire cloud would be much higher. Even if the SMBH seed did manage to form, the radiative pressure it would emit (plus mechanical feedback from the disk and jets) would slow the accretion rate, significantly slowing further growth.

Sources indicate that whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. As he said in a University of Portsmouth press release:.

It has been revealed that LRDs have been one of the most surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope. They are compact, only a few hundred light-years across, but are as bright as much larger galaxies, and their unusual V-shaped spectra have defied the usual astrophysical explanations. Their lack of detectable X-ray and radio emissions has left astronomers struggling to explain what they are.

Sources indicate that artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser.

Based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. What's more, their model suggests that the black holes are largely concealed by dense, massive discs of the gas that created them. These gaseous envelopes trap high-energy X-rays while allowing some visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light to escape, which fits with the unusual light signatures detected by the JWST.

It has been revealed that the simulations also explain another long-standing mystery about LRDs: that a large cluster of stars in the disks of these small galaxies produces the blue part of the spectrum Webb observed. These disks, according to the models, contain around 100 million stars densely packed into regions measuring only 500 light-years in diameter, matching what astronomers observed in LRDs. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses.

According to recent reports, this is a few orders of magnitude less than previous estimates, which indicated a maximum of 100 million Solar masses. While this research is unlikely to be the final word on the nature of LRDs, it offers what is (to date) the most fitting explanation that matches the observations. "What makes this discovery so exciting is that we may be witnessing the birth of the first supermassive black holes," remarked Whalen. "For decades, simulations have predicted that these objects should exist, and now the James Webb Space Telescope may finally be allowing us to see them.".

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth, The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

A Major Review Reveals Three Antidepressants That May Outperform Prozac

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.
  • A upcoming review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A massive review of 30,000 people suggests three antidepressants may outperform Prozac, but the findings reveal how much remains unknown about long-term depression treatment.

A upcoming review has found that some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found that people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta), and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

It has been revealed that treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an notable part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants, so it’s vital this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Sources indicate that studies of real-world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

According to recent reports, the latest review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six studies followed participants for longer than six months.

Recent findings suggest that this means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is notable given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

It has been revealed that people respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Recent findings suggest that continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects, and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing, or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

Industry News: Microscopic Space Dust Reveals A Hidden Reservoir Of "Heavy Water" Beyond Neptune

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects.
  • According to recent reports, in this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors.
  • It has been revealed that in 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that showed the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects. That was certainly the case recently when twelve dust grains collected by a high-altitude aircraft helped solve a mystery about the birth of our Solar System. Or at least that is the argument in a upcoming paper published in Science Advances by researchers at NASAâs Johnson Space Center and UCLA. According to the paper, the region beyond Neptune once had a massive isolated reservoir of âheavy waterâ that never mixed in with the inner planets.

According to recent reports, in this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors. Instead, it refers to a heavier version of the other element in good old H2O - oxygen. Most of the universeâs oxygen atoms are an isotope called oxygen-16, with eight protons and eight neutrons. However, a small percentage weighs in a bit heavier - oxygen-17 and oxygen-18, which carry an extra neutron or two, respectively.

It has been revealed that in 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that showed the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16. However, Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt seemed to have much more of the heavier oxygen isotopes. Which meant thereâs a mismatch between what we see inside the Sun and what the planets were formed out of. Scientists have been attempting to explain why for years.

Fraser explains the important of cosmic dust to life on Earth.

The most common explanation of why is known as carbon monoxide self-shielding. Around 4.5 billion years ago, when our Solar System hadnât fully formed yet, ultraviolet light from the Sun blew apart carbon monoxide molecules at the outer edges of the protoplanetary disk of gas and dust. Because oxygen-16 was the most prominent in the disk, the carbon monoxide particles that were made out of it would absorb much of the UV light that was directed at the disk, breaking the ones that were closest the light source (i.e. the Sun) apart. They eventually reformed with hydrogen to make âregularâ water.

In a recent development, however, that left other wavelengths of UV free to travel into the farther reaches of the protoplanetary disk. And some of those wavelengths were particularly good at breaking apart carbon monoxide molecules that had formed with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. So, in the outer disk, those heavier isotopes made up a higher percentage of the free-floating ions that eventually bonded to hydrogen, in their case creating âheavyâ water.

That makes sense from a theoretical standpoint at least, but proving this âheavy waterâ reservoir exists has been tricky. Almost all the meteorites we have found were formed in the main asteroid belt - not far enough out to capture particles of the reservoir. Some cometary sample missions, such as Rosetta and Stardust, have tried to capture water samples from these ambassadors of the outer solar system, but their method of capture resulted in the water-bearing materials melting, leaving no trace of their isotopic configuration.

Fraser explains the Kuiper Belt.

In a recent development, enter the fresh paper. Lead author Lindsay Keller and his team turned to interplanetary dust particles (IDPs). These microscopic grains are formed when comets and other icy bodies out in the Kuiper belt, the area past Neptune, collide and break apart. Some of the grains that result from those collisions are pulled inward by the Sunâs gravity, eventually intersecting the orbits of the inner planets - including Earth.

During their journey, they are subjected to extreme amounts of high energy particles from solar flares, which leaves microscopic scars on them called solar energetic particle tracks. Previous studies had proven that one way to prove a piece of dust had traveled from the Kuiper Belt is that have around a hundred times more energetic particle tracks, due to their much longer time in interplanetary space, than particles from asteroids do. In other words, if you can count the radiation tracks, you can prove whether a grain of dust came from beyond Neptune or not.

According to recent reports, that is exactly what they proved with twelve dust grains collected during NASAâs Cosmic Dust program - an ongoing airborne sampling program running out of Johnson Space Center since 1981. Shockingly, the collected particles still had lots of clays, like saponite, which are made with water, as well as iron-nickel sulfides and around four times as much carbon as would be expected for a primitive meteorite. The minerals proved that liquid water once flowed inside its parent Kuiper Belt object, either heated by radioactive decay or the kinetic energy of another impact.

Using a specialized microscope, the researchers measured the exact oxygen isotope ratios in the clays in the samples. They then worked back through chemical modeling to determine the original recipe for the water on the parent rock that formed the grains. They found that the primordial Kuiper Belt objects these grains came from were extraordinarily enriched with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18 - definitively proving that the reservoir of heavy water does exist out beyond Neptune.

Fraser talks about how there was liquid water on the asteroid Ryugu.

Recent findings suggest that as a consequence, they also, tangentially, provided a significant bump to the carbon monoxide self-shielding theory. And also noted the similarities to a specific unusual meteorite known as Acfer 094, which they hint might actually be a meteor from the Kuiper Belt itself. But there was one final mystery the paper needed to resolve - if there was all this heavy water out in the outer solar system, why didnât it migrate in when the planets were forming?

Industry observers note that the authors offer a simple explanation - Saturn. As Saturn grew in the early solar system, its gravity created a high-pressure ridge in the protoplanetary disk, acting as an invisible barrier to keep lightweight material from being pulled too far in towards the Sun. So, thanks to around a dozen specks of dust, we now have a more clearly defined picture of what our solar system looked like in the very early days of its formation - and it seems we can thank our giant ringed neighbor for some of how Earth ended up with its current isotopic balance.

L. Keller et al - A primordial heavy water reservoir in the outer solar system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

According to recent reports, this is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a fresh study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

According to recent reports, at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

According to recent reports, the gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

It has been revealed that origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its major flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

In a recent development, I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

Semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, intends to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the swiftly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

Sources indicate that when I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll promptly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot.
  • Sources indicate that the âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot.
  • In a recent development, but why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. Weâve always had trouble measuring them in the âmega-electron voltâ (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the âMeV gapâ. But a newly introduced paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration recently published a paper in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series that takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20-200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

Sources indicate that the âgapâ comes from a technological blind spot. Scientists have plenty of tools in the lower energy spectra, such as the Chandra X-ray observatory, that can capture radiation at the x-ray end of the electromagnetic spectrum. They also have a great number of tools at the high end of gamma ray spectroscopy, including the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which is capable of finding higher end ones.

In a recent development, but why are low energy gamma rays so hard to catch? Gamma rays notoriously pass right through mirrors and every other attempt to reflect them. Telescopes like Fermi-LAT can be thought of more as particle detectors in orbit rather than traditional telescopes. They track what happens when a gamma-ray photon hits layers of tungsten and silicon inside their chassis.

Fraser explains what a Quasar is.

In a recent development, at high energies - around 1 giga-electron volt (GeV), the damage done to those layers is catastrophic enough to be able to trace a line back to a source. However, at the lower 20-200 MeV range, the photons scatter much more randomly, making it difficult to track where precisely they came from. Fermi-LAT is only capable of tracking a single 20 MeV photon to a patch of the sky about 20 degrees wide - more than forty times the size of the full moon. Combine that with a massive amount of background radiation caused by everything from the Sun to distant galaxies, and it can be a real pain to pick out the direction of any one particular source.

In a recent development, however, Fermi-LAT has been operating now for almost two decades, and with that much data thereâs some math that can help. The researchers combined 14 years worth of collected data with some advanced statistical modeling techniques to pinpoint 450 distinct gamma-ray sources, what they are calling the Second Catalog of Low-Energy Fermi-LAT Sources, or 2FLE. Cross-checking them with other radio, optical, and X-ray data showed known counterparts for 377 of those objects.

The vast majority of those objects - 325 of them - are far outside the Milky Way. Almost half of the entire group of objects consist of flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs), a very extreme type of active galactic nuclei. FSRQs represent a type of âblazarâ - a supermassive black hole that is pointing one of its twin jets of plasma directly at Earth. The 2FLE catalog confirms that FSRQ blazars pump out the majority of their energy at this 20-200 MeV spectral window.

Fraser and Pamela discuss the differnet "colors" of gamma rays.

Closer to home, the catalogue includes 52 sources from inside the Milky Way. Most of them are pulsars - the spinning leftovers left behind when a supermassive star explodes into a supernova. But one intriguing outlier was gamma rays that appear to be coming from M2, a globular cluster, which would mark the first time itâs ever been observed at gamma-ray energies.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the paper, though, are the 73 sources that donât have a clear counterpart at other energies. 60 of those appear to be brand latest gamma-ray discoveries. And while some of those signals might turn out to be overlapping signals from neighboring objects, it's likely there are at least some truly new exotic cosmic accelerators in the dataset awaiting follow-up observations. One particular mystery source seems to align with an object called 2FLE J0340.8+5258, which seems to also have been detected by an observatory in China, and appears to be capable of generating light across nine orders of magnitude in energy.

Fermi-LAT itself seems to have reached its limit with this latest data set. The researchers have likely squeezed everything they could out of the decades of data of this satellite, which was originally introduced in 2008. However, there are other gamma-ray missions coming online, including NASAâs Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), which is designed specifically to look for gamma rays in the 0.2-5 MeV range using a special type of germanium detector that has only become available in the last few years. Combining that new data with the decades worth of Fermi might finally shed some light on one of the longest-standing blind spots in the extreme physics of the universe.

Cerebral Palsy May Not Be What Scientists Thought It Was

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that fresh research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP).
  • Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics, the research also proposes a different way to classify CP.
  • It has been revealed that cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fresh research is challenging how scientists understand cerebral palsy (CP). Of 515 genes previously linked to the condition, only 89 showed a statistically significant association in a new study, suggesting that many proposed genetic connections still lack sufficient evidence.

Published in the journal American Journal of Human Genetics, the research also proposes a different way to classify CP. Rather than treating it as a single disorder, the scientists suggest it may be better understood as a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions.

It has been revealed that cerebral palsy is the most common motor disability in children, with up to 10,000 babies diagnosed in the United States annually. It has traditionally been associated with complications around birth, including premature delivery and temporary oxygen deprivation. However, genetic research over the past decade has increasingly pointed to inherited or newly occurring genetic variants as potential contributors. Unlike progressive neurological diseases, CP does not worsen over time, and rehabilitation and physical therapy can improve symptoms.

“There has been a lack of consensus on the definition of cerebral palsy and on the role of genetics in disease pathogenesis, leading to substantial variability in whether a child is diagnosed with CP,” states corresponding author Peter Robinson of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine and the Berlin Institute of Health at Charité.

In a recent development, “We have developed a paradigm that considers CP to be a phenotypic trait rather than a precise disease diagnosis. A better understanding of specific genetic variants has the potential to improve our understanding of the biology of the disease.”.

To investigate the genetic basis of CP, the researchers evaluated evidence from 21 previously published studies involving 5,440 people diagnosed with the condition. These studies had identified potentially causal variants across hundreds of genes, but the fresh statistical analysis found convincing evidence of association for only a fraction of them.

“We decided to do this study because there has been no accepted statistical method to determine if a disease-associated gene is truly linked to CP,” says first author Adam Arterbery of the Jackson Laboratory for Genomic Medicine. “We discovered it was extremely difficult to find statistical evidence of causality for many of the genetic variants previously linked to CP.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team also performed whole-genome sequencing on 460 children from 453 families receiving care at Shriners Children’s hospitals across the United States. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic genetic variants were identified in 70 families, spanning 60 genes. However, just 16 of those genes overlapped with the genes supported by statistically significant evidence in the analysis of earlier studies.

According to recent reports, the researchers emphasize that their findings do not disprove connections between CP and the remaining genes. Instead, the available data are insufficient to establish those associations with statistical confidence. They propose viewing CP as a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences, rather than a single disease with a common biological origin.

Sources indicate that “This framework could improve interpretation of genomic testing, help identify children who may warrant closer CP surveillance or specialist referral, and potentially identify genetic conditions requiring disease-specific management,” Robinson indicates. “But clinical utility and patient benefit will absolutely need validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.”.

It has been revealed that future studies will focus on larger patient populations, prospective evaluations of clinical benefits and costs, and better access to genomic and medical data. “We hope our study will stimulate discussion about CP terminology, gene-disease associations, and variant interpretation,” Arterbery indicates. “The most productive response will be further validation and development of better genotype-phenotype evidence rather than treating the findings as a definitive list of CP genes.”.

#111696. Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1550 w)

Extremely Accurate Measurements of a Pair of Flaring Red Dwarfs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity.
  • According to recent reports, one fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger.
  • The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About 59 light years away, a binary pair of red dwarfs are orbiting a common center of gravity. Unlike stars like our Sun, which are relatively radio-quiet, red dwarfs (M dwarfs) can produce strong radio emissions. A team of astronomers used that to their advantage to take precision measurements of a binary pair of M dwarfs about 59 million light years from Earth. They determined the stars' orbits and masses with uncommon accuracy.

According to recent reports, one fundamental fact about low and intermediate mass stars, including M dwarfs, is that they rotate more rapidly when they're younger. Stars inherit angular momentum from their formation in gas clouds, and since M dwarfs are so small, that momentum is concentrated, making them spin rapidly. They eventually slow down, but this initial rapid rotation makes them very active.

The fast rotation generates powerful magnetic dynamos, and young M dwarfs exhibit very large sunspots and more frequent, powerful stellar flares.

One subset of young M dwarfs is even more extreme. They're called Complex Periodic Variable (CPV) stars, and they're very young, between about 10 and 100 million years old. They're M dwarfs that display complex, periodical optical light curves with sharp drops rather than smooth drops found in most stellar light curves. Their drops aren't simple; there can be multiple dips and peaks during a single rotation. Astrophysicists call their light curves multi-harmonic, and the patterns repeat across multiple rotations.

It has been revealed that this image demonstrates CPV light curves for three typical CPV stars found by TESS. Notice the sharp drops in the curves rather than typical smooth drops found in other stellar light curves. Image Credit: Bouma et al. 2023. AnJ.

The binary system in this research is named DG CVn, and one of them is a CPV star. Though CPV stars have complex light curves generated by their youthful, rapid rotation, their youthfulness also means they're radio loud. In fact, since both of these stars are young M dwarfs, they're both radio loud. That helped the researchers measure them with such accuracy.

The measurments of DG CVn are in newly introduced research in Astronomy and Astrophysics titled "Accurate dynamical mass and orbit determination of the M dwarf binary DG CVn using astrometric very long baseline interferometry." The lead author is Paul VLBI , a network system engineer at the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry ERIC (JIVE), and a Leiden Observatory PhD student. It's noteworthy that this is the first mass measurement of a system with a CPV star.

"We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star." - Boven et al. 2026.

The astronomers' results are based on observations that spanned 18 years. Observations with the National Science Foundationâs Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) between 2023 and 2025 were especially vital in their precise results. The VLBA is a system of 10 radiotelescopes across the USA, each one measuring 25 meters. The 10 dishes work as an interferometer, and the VLBA has the longest baseline in the world, up to 8,611 km long.

According to recent reports, "Astrometry through very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) allows the monitoring of radio-loud stars and the detection of any reflex motion due to stellar or substellar companions," the authors write. Reflex motion is the characteristic gravitational wobble induced in a star when a companion tugs on it.

Sources indicate that that wobble is often used to detect unseeable exoplanets orbiting stars. Even a small planet can make its star wobble, and that's at the heart of the radial velocity method of detecting exoplanet. The DG CVn system was actually found when astronomers were searching for exoplanets with the radial velocity method. But the system exhibited a more powerful and complex wobble than an exoplanet would.

Recent findings suggest that âWe were really lucky to hear about this object when we had developed tools with which we could explain these motions,â said Boven. âBut the real surprise came when we also detected the second radio-loud dwarf in the observations we did to confirm our model. It really allowed us to measure the system very precisely.â.

Measuring reflex motion accurately with the VLBI let the astronomers track the stars' paths, including the tiny wobbles, which in turn let them understand the mass of the stars with extreme precision.

This figure from the research shows the VLBI detections of both members of DG CVn, and their modeled motion across the sky. The dates mark the predicted positions of DG CVn B over time. The inset image shows recent observations when both sources were detected. Image Credit: Boven et al. 2026. A&A.

In a recent development, "In our recent observations, we reliably detected both binary components," the authors write. "A unique and accurate determination of the 1647.647 Â± 0.027 day orbit, with a parallax distance of 18.1851 Â± 0.0033 pc (about 59 light years), is presented. The dynamical masses were estimated with a precision of 0.16% from the sampled posteriors.".

The pair of stars orbit each other every 4.511 years on an elongated elliptical orbit. When they're closest to one another, they're only separated by 0.59 astronomical units. DG CVn A is the more massive of the pair with 0.39 solar masses, while DG CVn B has 0.36 solar masses. The pair is close enough to measure their distance with parallax, which gives accurate measurements.

In a recent development, the red dwarfs and their radio emissions are central to this work. The stars are simply too close together from this distance to be separated in optical observations. But the VLBA can pinpoint their locations with extreme accuracy. All of this work let the researchers characterize the system in clear detail, following the motions of both stars through the sky separately.

It has been revealed that âDG CVn is a beautiful example of what precise radio astrometry can reveal,â stated Jay Blanchard, NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory astronomer and study co-author. âBy following these two stars over many years, we can see their orbital motion directly and use that motion to determine properties that would otherwise be extremely difficult to measure.â.

These accurate measurements also tell astronomers about their planetary systems. Planets form in protoplanetary disks around stars, and since these stars are so close together, that limits the size of their disks. Smaller disks mean smaller planets, so that limits the size of any exoplanets in the system. It's also extremely unlikely that any long-period planets are orbiting either star.

Sources indicate that according to the researchers' estimates, an exoplanet in orbit around one of the stars could only be in a stable orbit if its orbital period was less than approximately 23 days. For a circumbinary planet orbiting both stars, the orbital period would have to be at least about 36 years. These approximations are also notable, because they can refine the understanding of how exoplanets can form and survive in binary star systems.

Gaia's Data Release 4 is due in a couple of weeks, and it will include binary star parameters for the mission's complete survey. But that data alone won't be able to differentiate between binaries where both are low mass stars, and binaries where one might be a massive planet. But the VLBI will be able to address that. "Astrometric follow-up of selected detections with VLBI can help to differentiate between binary star systems and reflex motion due to large exoplanets (or even both)," the authors write.

Recent findings suggest that "We have presented a complete binary orbital solution with high accuracy based on VLBI astrometry of a binary that is difficult to resolve for optical telescopes on the ground or in orbit," the authors write. "The absolute astrometry provided by VLBI allowed the individual dynamical masses to be determined with high accuracy. These results show that VLBI is well suited for studying the orbits of radio-loud stars.".

The results also show how powerful the combination of archival observations and new observations can be. "The value of combining archival and recent VLBI astrometric observations has been demonstrated. It resulted in a highly accurate determination of the system composition, orbit, position, and distance," the authors write. "We present the first dynamical mass measurement of a binary containing a CPV star.".

The VLBI network of radio dishes is about to have a growth spurt when the Square Kilometre Array and the Next Generation Very Large Array come online. That will improve the system's reach and precision.

According to recent reports, "In the future, we hope to make measurements precise enough to detect planets in orbit around such radio-loud dwarfs,â noted Huib van Langevelde, chief scientist a the Joint Institute for Very Long Baseline Interferometry and Leiden Observatory professor. âWe think that when the ngVLA and the SKA become part of the VLBI network, we can do even more precise measurements, for many more, more distant stars.â.

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (645 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District.
  • Recent findings suggest that north Carolina Rep.
  • Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that north Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

Industry observers note that “[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”.

Industry observers note that hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a latest GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

Sources indicate that north Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.
  • In a recent development, deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unusual sea creature survives with much of its digestive system missing, thanks to a remarkable partnership with bacteria that could offer new clues about how life evolves.

In a recent development, deep beneath the seafloor, where sunlight never reaches and oxygen is almost nonexistent, scientists have discovered an unusual relationship that may help explain how marine life survives in some of Earth’s most extreme environments. A deep-sea mollusk living in the South China Sea contains a previously unknown cellular structure packed with bacteria, offering newly introduced clues about how animals adapt to conditions that would be inhospitable to most other species.

According to recent reports, the discovery adds to a growing understanding of cold seep ecosystems, where life depends on chemical energy rather than sunlight. These environments contain abundant methane and hydrogen sulfide, which certain bacteria can use to support their metabolism. Animals such as deep-sea mussels, clams, and tubeworms have evolved close relationships with these microbes, providing them with shelter inside their cells in exchange for nutrients.

Until now, however, scientists had found no clear evidence that animals could develop specialized organelles dedicated to maintaining these bacterial partnerships.

Industry observers note that the upcoming research centers on Chaetoderma shenloong, also known as the Divine Dragon Glistenworm. This unusual mollusk belongs to the aplacophoran class Caudofoveata and can grow to more than 150 millimeters (nearly 6 inches) long, far larger than most of its relatives. Its distinctive characteristics earned it recognition as one of the “Top-Ten Marine Species of 2024.”.

It has been revealed that researchers found that the animal spends much of its life buried tens of centimeters beneath the seafloor, in sediment rich in hydrogen sulfide and containing almost no oxygen. Understanding how it survives there led the team to examine an unexpected feature of its anatomy.

Using anatomical analysis, micro-computed tomography, and three-dimensional imaging, the scientists discovered that Chaetoderma shenloong has a digestive system unlike those of most mollusks. Its radula, a feeding structure commonly used by mollusks, is heavily reduced, while its midgut, hindgut, and anus have almost completely disappeared.

Recent findings suggest that instead, an extensive system of digestive glands occupies most of its body cavity. These glands contain enormous numbers of symbiotic bacteria that serve as the animal’s primary source of nutrients and energy.

Closer examination revealed something even more unusual inside the glands.

Sources indicate that the bacteria were concentrated within spherical structures measuring approximately 10 to 15 micrometers across. Each structure was enclosed by more than 20 layers of membrane and contained hundreds to thousands of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria. The researchers named this structure the dracosphera, Latin for “dragon ball,” because of its beadlike shape and surrounding layers.

Recent findings suggest that A single host cell accommodated more than 1,600 bacterial symbionts on average. The dracosphera also lacked familiar cellular components, including host nuclei and lysosomes, distinguishing it from an ordinary cell or a typical digestive compartment.

This arrangement suggests that the mollusk may have developed a specialized structure for housing and maintaining its bacterial partners, potentially representing a previously unrecognized form of cooperation between animals and microorganisms.

The scientists then investigated how this relationship might function in an environment where oxygen is so scarce.

Genomic analyses of Chaetoderma shenloong and its symbiotic bacteria revealed that the microbes possess adaptations allowing them to maintain their metabolism with very little oxygen. The mollusk, meanwhile, lives deep in the sediment to obtain chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide that its bacterial partners can use.

That creates a difficult balance. The animal and its microbes must obtain the chemicals needed to sustain their partnership while coping with the severe shortage of oxygen in the surrounding mud.

One possibility is that the dracosphera’s many membrane layers help manage how oxygen moves through the animal’s body. The researchers propose that these layers could slow oxygen diffusion, allowing limited supplies to be directed preferentially toward the mollusk’s own cells while still supporting its bacterial partners.

For now, this explanation remains a hypothesis that requires further testing.

The team also found evidence suggesting that the dracosphera participates in nutrient exchange. Digestion-related cellular structures and signs of enzyme activity were abundant around the regions containing symbiotic bacteria. These observations suggest that the mollusk may obtain essential nutrients it cannot produce itself by breaking down some of its bacterial partners.

Beyond explaining how one unusual animal survives, the findings may offer insight into a much older biological process.

Recent findings suggest that scientists believe that mitochondria, which occur in animal and plant cells, and chloroplasts, found in plant cells, originated through ancient relationships between microorganisms and their hosts. Over evolutionary time, these partnerships gave rise to structures that became essential components of complex cells.

Sources indicate that the dracosphera does not establish that a similar evolutionary transition is occurring in Chaetoderma shenloong. However, its distinctive organization provides researchers with another example of how intimately animals and bacteria can cooperate, potentially helping scientists investigate how specialized organelles and new cellular functions evolve.

The discovery could also have implications for understanding the broader deep-sea ecosystem.

Researchers identified traces of Chaetoderma shenloong at the mud volcano cold seep off Kyushu, Japan, and the Site F cold seep in the northern South China Sea. Together with previous records of large, closely related species in the Gulf of Mexico, these observations raise the possibility that animals with similar bacterial partnerships are more widely distributed across deep-sea cold seeps than currently recognized.

According to recent reports, such organisms may participate in the movement and transformation of methane, sulfur, and carbon within these ecosystems. Establishing their distribution and ecological contributions could help scientists better understand how life operates in parts of the ocean that remain poorly explored.

Reference: “A multilamellar organelle for chemosymbiosis in an aplacophoran mollusc adapted to anoxic cold seep sediment” by Yunlong Li, Chong Chen, Xu Liu, Menggong Li, Guoyong Yan, Haiyun Zhou, Hui Wang, Xiaoshan Zheng, Xing He, Shanshan Liu, Jian-Wen Qiu, Pei-Yuan Qian and Jin Sun, 30 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78965-0.

The work also received support from the National Key Research and Development Program of China, the Laoshan Laboratory, the Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province, the Guangzhou Laboratory and research funds from the HKSAR Government, among other sources.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the âgas giantsâ made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the âice giantsâ, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giantâs thick atmospheres.

According to recent reports, scientists are getting excited because there has been an ongoing debate that these distant worlds are actually covered in rock. But we canât simply fly a probe out a few billion miles and drill down into their surfaces to determine that for ourselves. Instead, they decided to use proxies, such as the concentration of argon-40, as a rough measurement for how much rock there is below the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that understanding why the presence of one noble gas isotope leads to understanding whether rock is present or not requires a bit of a diversion into the world of bananas. Or at least, it gives me an excuse to talk about bananas in a planetary science article. Bananas are radioactive, and the thing causing their radioactivity is potassium-40 - a relatively unstable form of a very common element. When potassium-40 decays, it turns into argon-40, which, as a noble gas, hardly interacts with anything.

Fraser talks about how to plan a mission to Uranus.

In a recent development, most of this radioactive decay takes place in rocks containing potassium-40, rather than bananas, so one of the most common sources of argon-40 is literally rocks. After it is created, it bubbles up out of those rocks and escapes into its host planetâs atmosphere. In fact, it makes up around 1% of the air youâre breathing right now.

On the ice giants, this same process could hold - argon-40 could form inside a rocky surface, and then bubble up into the planetâs atmosphere over billions of years. So we should be able to send a probe to measure the concentration of argon-40 in their atmospheres, and that would serve as an effective proxy for the existence of rock under the atmosphere.

Thereâs just one catch - rocks arenât really the only source of argon-40. In fact, there was already plenty of it floating around in the protosolar nebula that the Sun and all the planets eventually formed out of. Therefore, Uranus and Neptune could have âtrappedâ this leftover argon-40 before they were even mature, causing argon-40 to eventually appear in their atmosphere, but not from rocky surfaces.

Fraser talks about efforts to go back to visit the ice giants of the solar system.

According to recent reports, according to the paper, the amount of argon collected by the early versions of Neptune and Uranus depends entirely on where they formed with regards to the âargon ice lineâ. This line, which happens around 23-35 Kelvin, the temperature that argon freezes into solid ice, or is trapped inside water ice, is the determining factor of how much primordial argon Neptune and Uranus had sucked up.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, thereâs still a lot of debate about where exactly in the solar system the ice giants formed. If they formed close to the Sun and eventually migrated back out to the edges of the solar system, they might not have captured much argon ice, and the majority of the argon in their atmospheres would be due to release from rocks. On the other hand, if the theories about them actively moving through the solar system soon after their creation are true, then they would likely have captured a large amount of argon-40, making it useless as an indicator of whether or not the planets have a rocky surface.

In a recent development, luckily, there is a way to potentially solve this puzzle. Argon-40 has a lighter isotopic cousin, known as argon-36, which is non-radioactive, and doesnât form in decaying rocks. Measuring its level would act like a control group, allowing scientists to estimate how much of the argon present in the atmosphere would have been swallowed at birth, as we have other estimates of the ratio between argon-40 and argon-36 in the early solar system.

Itâs good these sorts of insights are coming out now, as there is right now a mission, Uranus Orbiter and Probe, which is in active development and planned to arrive in the system in the 2040s. That still gives us some time to finalize our theories about what we would expect to find there. And perhaps, once it does arrive, weâll be able to definitively answer whether or not the âIce giantsâ have a truly solid surface or not.

Scientists Finally Solve the 1,700-Year-Old Mystery of 8,000 Dead Frogs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.
  • Recent findings suggest that finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway.
  • Sources indicate that nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forests cleared for livestock in Roman Britain may have made young frogs more vulnerable to owls, revealing how human activity shaped wildlife nearly 1,700 years ago.

Recent findings suggest that finding 8,000 frog bones buried in a single ditch raised a strange question for archaeologists working along England’s A14 highway. What had killed so many frogs, and why had their remains accumulated in one place? Evidence that the ditch filled within just one year made the discovery even more puzzling.

Sources indicate that nearly a decade later, researchers from Bournemouth University and Museum of London Archaeology (MOLA) believe they have identified the culprits. The frogs were likely eaten by birds of prey, particularly short-eared owls and hen harriers, that took advantage of a landscape transformed by human activity during the Roman period.

The bones were uncovered between 2016 and 2018 during the National Highways A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. After learning about the discovery through news reports, Dr. Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University contacted Dr. Vicki Ewens, a senior zooarchaeologist at MOLA, to investigate.

Industry observers note that clarkson compared damage on the ancient bones with patterns documented in previous studies and found evidence that the frogs had been eaten by birds of prey. Although this helped identify the likely predators, it did not fully explain how so many remains had collected in such a short time.

A closer examination of the frogs’ ages offered another clue. Using a pioneering method based on measuring their humeri, or upper arm bones, the researchers determined that most had died young, during the winter of their first year of life. Radiocarbon dating conducted by the University of Vienna placed the remains approximately 1,700 years ago, during the Roman period.

At the time, Fen waters were retreating from the valley, creating favorable conditions for frogs to breed. This would have provided a plentiful food source for birds hunting in the area. Changes to the surrounding landscape may have made the young frogs even more vulnerable.

According to recent reports, short-eared owls typically hunt over grassland, yet the valley had been wooded during the Iron Age. To understand how the environment changed, researchers examined evidence from snails, pollen, and charcoal. Their findings demonstrated that substantial areas of woodland had gradually been cleared to create grazing land for livestock.

By the Roman period, large stretches of open ground had replaced much of the woodland. With fewer trees providing cover, frogs would have been more exposed to predators hunting across the grassland.

“We don’t often get an owl’s-eye view of what it was like in the past from archaeological sites,” stated Clarkson, who led the study.

According to recent reports, “The mystery of these frogs has been solved – a feast of frogs that were eaten and their bones left behind by a group of owls. These bones not only tell us about life for people living near the Roman Fens, but they also give insights into the natural world – what wild animals were getting up to in the past, and what life was like for them,” he added.

Sources indicate that the findings may also offer clues about how people used the valley during Roman times. Researchers suggest that communities may have visited the area seasonally to move livestock between grazing pastures. A less crowded landscape could have provided favorable conditions for hunting birds, although this connection remains a possible explanation rather than a confirmed finding.

What began as an unusual collection of animal remains has therefore helped researchers reconstruct both the changing environment and the activities of people who lived near the Roman Fens.

As Ewens concludes, “I had so many theories as to why such a large collection of frog bones was recovered from this small feature. It’s been great to collaborate with Paul to finally answer this question. This research shows how even the smallest animal recovered on a site can help us to understand not only past environmental conditions but human activity within a wider landscape.”.

Reference: “An Owl’s Eye View: Human–Animal Entanglement at the Roman Fen Edge” by Paul Clarkson, Vicki Ewens, Owain Scholma-Mason, Ellen Hambleton, Peter Andrews and Emma Jenkins, 17 October 2026, Environmental Archaeology. DOI: 10.1080/14614103.2026.2746302.

In a recent development, national Highways funded the archaeological works for the A14 Cambridge to Huntingdon Improvement Scheme. Funding was provided by Bournemouth University post-graduate support grant for material retrieval, researcher travel, and radiocarbon dating.
