📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

Luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

It has been revealed that this artist's illustration shows the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

Dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

Dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

Industry observers note that âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â said Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

According to recent reports, this image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and reveals the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

Euclid launched in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Massive Bang.

According to recent reports, among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

Euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 new strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

In a recent development, "Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â remarked Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 newly introduced candidates.â.

Recent findings suggest that there's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row demonstrates, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

Recent findings suggest that overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â noted Srivastava.

According to recent reports, strong gravitational lensing is an vital tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

In a recent development, finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly key in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang model of cosmology.

It has been revealed that lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Recent findings suggest that euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one big grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each new data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

According to recent reports, but that won't be the end of cosmology. Newly introduced questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever upcoming ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Sources indicate that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

According to recent reports, why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

Industry observers note that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Industry observers note that nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Sources indicate that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

In a recent development, this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated promptly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be remarked is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Newly introduced Research Finds Common ADHD Classroom Accommodations May Not Actually Help

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For children with ADHD, the support they receive at school may not always make the difference parents and teachers hope for.
  • Giving children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) more time to finish assignments, frequent breaks, or a quieter place to work might seem like straightforward ways to help them succeed in school.
  • A study from Florida International University (FIU), published in JAMA Pediatrics, found that four common accommodations did not produce significant improvements in children with ADHD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For children with ADHD, the support they receive at school may not always make the difference parents and teachers hope for.

Giving children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) more time to finish assignments, frequent breaks, or a quieter place to work might seem like straightforward ways to help them succeed in school. These adjustments are widely used in classrooms, yet new research suggests they may do little to improve academic performance or behavior.

A study from Florida International University (FIU), published in JAMA Pediatrics, found that four common accommodations did not produce significant improvements in children with ADHD. The results raise questions about how schools support students whose difficulties with attention, behavior, and completing schoolwork can interfere with their education.

“We were surprised that none of the accommodations we tested had a significant effect, even when combined with behavioral interventions or medication,” said Gregory Fabiano, a psychology professor at FIU and the study’s lead author.

It has been revealed that researchers at FIU’s Center for Children and Families conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 255 children with ADHD, ranging from kindergarten through sixth grade. The children entered the study between 2022 and 2025, and 235 completed it.

The research took place through FIU’s Summer Treatment Program, which provides structured classroom and recreational activities for children with ADHD.

Sources indicate that researchers tested four accommodations commonly offered in schools: extended time on assignments, frequent breaks, standing while working at a desk, and completing work in a low-distraction environment. They measured how these adjustments affected classroom rule violations, academic productivity, and quiz scores under different treatment conditions.

The results revealed clear differences between the commonly used accommodations and treatments designed to address ADHD symptoms:.

Sources indicate that the distinction matters because schools frequently include accommodations in Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) and Section 504 plans, which are designed to meet students’ individual educational needs. Although these adjustments may make classroom tasks more manageable for some children, the findings suggest that routinely providing them does not necessarily improve measurable academic outcomes or behavior.

“These approaches fail to build skills or address motivation,” Fabiano stated.

According to recent reports, rather than relying heavily on accommodations, researchers recommend placing greater emphasis on behavioral strategies supported by evidence. These include setting clear expectations, providing consistent feedback, praising positive behavior, and rewarding students for meeting personalized goals.

One approach is the use of daily report cards, which allow teachers to monitor specific behaviors and give students regular feedback on their progress.

The findings do not mean accommodations are never useful. Individual students may benefit from particular adjustments, even if those approaches did not produce significant improvements across the children studied.

“There may be times when accommodations may be helpful, but a ‘one size fits all’ approach to ADHD doesn’t seem to be effective,” he said.

The research builds on decades of work by the late William E. Pelham Jr., the founding director of FIU’s Center for Children and Families, who helped design and conduct the study.

A pioneer in ADHD treatment, Pelham also led landmark research showing that stimulant medication improved children’s classroom productivity without significantly improving how much they learned. That earlier finding highlights an crucial distinction between helping students complete schoolwork and helping them understand and retain information.

The latest study also has limitations. Researchers conducted the trial in structured summer treatment classrooms rather than ordinary schools, where classroom conditions, teaching practices, and available support may differ. Additional research is needed to determine whether the results hold in everyday educational settings.

For Fabiano, the findings underscore the need to reconsider which forms of support schools prioritize for children with ADHD.

It has been revealed that “We need to rethink how we’re supporting these students, with greater emphasis on effective treatments in everyday classrooms rather than relying so heavily on accommodations. Every child with ADHD deserves the opportunity to succeed and feel proud of what they’ve accomplished in the classroom, and it is our job to make sure we give them the best chance for that,” Fabiano noted.

Reference: “Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Accommodations, Behavior Therapy, and Stimulant Medication: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Gregory A. Fabiano, Brittany M. Merrill, Rosalia F. Gallo, Marcela Ramos, Morgan Jusko, Devon Tower, Elizabeth M. Gnagy, Amy Boeckel, Jennifer Piscitello, Maya Renaud, Alyssa Dawson, Jennifer Sikov, Carolina Ramirez, Grant C. Edmondson, Michael S. Adragna, Carlos A. Salgado and Timothy B. Hayes, 13 November 2026, JAMA Pediatrics. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.5973.

This study was funded by grant R01HD105318 awarded to Florida International University from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development. The infrastructure for the summer treatment program in Miami was funded in part by The Children’s Trust.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • According to recent reports, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

According to recent reports, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

Recent findings suggest that in the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

According to recent reports, however, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

According to recent reports, but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

But ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

A Chemical Signature Suddenly Disappeared From Earth’s Rocks. Scientists Think They Know Why

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have uncovered a mysterious chemical change in ancient rocks that reveals a major turning point in Earth’s geological history.
  • A chemical fingerprint preserved in some of Earth’s oldest rocks disappears from the geological record around 2.5 billion years ago.
  • Determining when plate tectonics emerged has been a longstanding challenge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have uncovered a mysterious chemical change in ancient rocks that reveals a major turning point in Earth’s geological history.

A chemical fingerprint preserved in some of Earth’s oldest rocks disappears from the geological record around 2.5 billion years ago. Researchers at Curtin University have traced this abrupt change across thousands of rock samples, identifying a major transition in how Earth’s crust formed and recycled. Their findings suggest that the planet was beginning to develop a tectonic system resembling the one operating today.

Determining when plate tectonics emerged has been a longstanding challenge. The movement of Earth’s tectonic plates continually reshapes continents and ocean basins, while recycling enormous amounts of crust into the planet’s interior. This process destroys much of the geological evidence needed to reconstruct its earliest history.

It has been revealed that the researchers investigated chemical signatures that can survive when older crust melts and contributes to the formation of upcoming rock. These signatures can help identify the original material from which younger rocks formed.

It has been revealed that “New crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” said lead author Dr. Janne Liebmann, a research fellow at Curtin University. “We searched for this fingerprint in thousands of rocks from around the world, spanning almost four billion years of Earth’s history.”.

“We found it consistently in rocks older than 2.5 billion years, showing they were derived from a pool of ancient crust that formed about four billion years ago.”.

“But after 2.5 billion years ago, that fingerprint disappears from the geological record, and despite examining thousands of rocks, we never see it again.”.

Sources indicate that the disappearance suggests that the processes responsible for generating newly introduced crust underwent a fundamental transformation. Rather than repeatedly melting and reworking ancient crust in place, Earth increasingly developed a system capable of transporting and recycling crust across much larger distances.

“That tells us something fundamental changed in the way Earth’s crust was being formed and transformed, marking a transition towards the dynamic tectonic system we see today,” Liebmann said.

Study co-author Professor Chris Kirkland, from Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, connected the findings to the geological processes that distinguish Earth from planets such as Venus and Mars, which lack a comparable global system of active plate tectonics.

“Plate tectonics is fundamental to the way Earth has evolved over billions of years, continually reshaping the continents and oceans and influencing the planet’s atmosphere and climate,” Kirkland stated.

“What makes this finding remarkable is that we can see the fingerprints of an ancient Earth disappear from the geological record at a very specific point in time.”.

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale.”.

The results identify a major change in crustal evolution around 2.5 billion years ago, although they do not establish that modern plate tectonics began suddenly or that all its defining features emerged simultaneously.

“This gives us our clearest geological evidence yet for when the tectonic engine that drives the modern Earth ‘switched on’.”.

Reference: “Loss of ancient crustal reservoirs marks a shift in Earth’s geodynamic regime” by Janne Liebmann, Christopher L. Kirkland, Michael I. H. Hartnady and Christopher J. Spencer, 1 November 2026, Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences. DOI: 10.1098/rspa.2026.0587.

Tech Report: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • Industry observers note that the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

Industry observers note that the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

According to recent reports, this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

Industry observers note that we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

According to recent reports, adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Upcoming to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

In a recent development, as Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Recent findings suggest that mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“major plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

According to recent reports, eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

According to recent reports, this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

According to recent reports, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the fresh template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

These days, London has no shortage of excellent fresh-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

Industry observers note that this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Latest York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Industry observers note that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

In a recent development, clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most notable British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

In a recent development, joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Recent findings suggest that given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

Chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

In a recent development, must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

According to recent reports, shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Recent findings suggest that bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

Industry observers note that for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy latest surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

In a recent development, gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Industry observers note that chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

According to recent reports, together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

According to recent reports, there’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

According to recent reports, A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

Industry observers note that this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

In his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips notes Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Recent findings suggest that bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

According to recent reports, fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

According to recent reports, must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • Industry observers note that earth is one substantial system.
  • In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a substantial part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Industry observers note that earth is one substantial system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a upcoming trick with them: photosynthesis.

In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

But this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

In a recent development, newly introduced research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

According to recent reports, the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

According to recent reports, the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research indicates that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

They found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

It has been revealed that the second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

In a recent development, the researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

It has been revealed that this graphic illustrates the results from fresh research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that highlights how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it indicates that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

According to recent reports, "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

This figure shows the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

According to recent reports, it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work demonstrates that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Industry observers note that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

It has been revealed that understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • Industry observers note that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Sources indicate that understanding why this is vital requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Industry observers note that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Sources indicate that understanding why this is vital requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

What was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study indicated that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

In a recent development, solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

Recent findings suggest that with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the latest paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.
