A Century-Old Pollution Disaster Has Been Discovered Frozen in Arctic Ice

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.
  • More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source.
  • Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decisions made at one Montana smelter may have shaped the air millions breathed, while Arctic ice reveals how much pollution earlier controls could have prevented.

More than a century ago, toxic pollution from a copper smelter in Montana was spreading across North America, reaching communities thousands of miles from its source. Much of that contamination went unmeasured at the time, but traces of it survived in an unexpected place: Arctic ice.

Scientists have now used those frozen records to uncover how one industrial operation may have exposed millions of people to harmful levels of arsenic and lead. The findings also demonstrate how the Earth’s ice preserves evidence of human activity long after pollution has disappeared from the air.

Industry observers note that the study, published November 10 in Nature Sustainability, was led by Joe McConnell and Nathan Chellman of the Desert Research Institute (DRI), alongside international collaborators. The team examined 10 ice cores from Greenland, northern Canada, and the Russian Arctic, finding that concentrations of toxic metals in some locations rose to approximately 15 times preindustrial levels between 1886 and 1918.

The evidence pointed to the Anaconda Copper Mine complex near Butte, Montana, one of the world’s largest copper producers at the time. Researchers estimated that during its peak production decades, the operation released approximately 11,000 tons of arsenic and 4,400 tons of lead into the atmosphere each year.

“It’s pretty wild to think that a single, albeit massive source of pollution could have affected effectively the entire North American continent and western Greenland more than 4000 kilometers or 2500 miles away,” McConnell stated.

Using historical census records and models of atmospheric pollution, the researchers estimated that approximately 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic concentrations associated with increased risks of lung cancer and other serious illnesses.

Industry observers note that people living near the operation faced particularly high exposure. For nearly 30 years, residents of Montana and parts of Wyoming and Idaho experienced arsenic concentrations that met or exceeded the World Health Organization’s current recommended maximum threshold for chronic exposure. The researchers also estimated that 1.4 million Americans and Canadians encountered elevated lead pollution potentially associated with cognitive effects equivalent to a 2.6-point reduction in IQ.

It has been revealed that although the study did not directly measure health outcomes, arsenic and lead exposure are associated with cancer, diabetes, cognitive decline, and heart disease. Pollution settling onto crops, soil, and water could also have created additional risks beyond those examined in the study.

To reconstruct this forgotten pollution, scientists turned to the Arctic’s natural record of atmospheric change. As snow accumulates, it traps tiny particles carried by the wind, including industrial pollutants. Over time, the snow becomes ice, preserving chemical evidence of conditions from decades or even centuries earlier.

Industry observers note that by comparing metal concentrations across the 10 ice cores, combining them with atmospheric models, and examining historical mining records, the researchers traced the contamination to northern North America. Arsenic measurements, supported by related chemical markers, closely matched Anaconda’s production history, while lead isotope evidence reinforced the connection.

Sources indicate that the timing also revealed how industrial decisions shaped the atmosphere. Copper demand surged during rapid electrification and the buildup to World War I, increasing pollution from ore processing. Near Anaconda, damaged crops, reduced harvests, and livestock deaths had already prompted decades of legal disputes.

After the organization installed pollution-control equipment around 1919, heavy-metal emissions declined by approximately 65%, according to the ice-core evidence. Similar technology had been available years earlier, but Anaconda delayed installation for roughly a decade.

The researchers calculated that installing those controls ten years sooner could have prevented another 60,000 tons of arsenic and 24,000 tons of lead from spreading across much of North America.

Recent findings suggest that the Arctic record captures both sides of that history. It reveals how pollution from one industrial site reached millions of people and how changes in industrial practices eventually reduced its impact. Even today, the ice preserves evidence of environmental damage that otherwise might have remained largely hidden.

Reference: “Widespread North American pollution and health impacts from early twentieth century copper production” by Joseph R. McConnell, Nathan J. Chellman, Sophie M. Wensman, Alison S. Criscitiello, Andreas Plach, Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, Diedrich Fritzsche, Kira M. Holland, Drake McCrimmon, Matthew B. Osman, John Sandlos and Andreas Stohl, 10 November 2026, Nature Sustainability. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01975-9.

#111662. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1894 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that binary stars are common in the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs).
  • In a recent development, it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that binary stars are common in the Milky Way. Up to 40% Milky Way stars are binaries, though there's a lack of absolute certainty. Sirius, which is the brightest star in the night sky, is actually a binary star.

Astronomers know that in some situations, binary stars share common envelopes (CEs). It means that a body of gas surrounds both stars, but the gas doesn't move with either one separately. These envelopes are transitory; the CE creates drag that slowly draws the planets together, sometimes ending in an explosion. But it's difficult to predict when that will happen, and when astronomers should observe a particular binary star to learn more about it.

In a recent development, it all begins with common envelope evolution (CEE), a critical stage in the evolution of binary stars. No two stars in a binary system are the same. One evolves and puffs up, overflowing its Roche lobe. Mass begins to pile up on its companion. That process becomes unstable, and the two stars become engulfed in a common envelope of gas.

In a recent development, the common envelope exerts a powerful drag on both stars, and they're drawn closer together. After that, the CE is ejected and the two stars are left behind in a compact binary. The pair of tightly-bound stars can remain as a compact binary, or they can merge and cause an explosion, called a luminous red nova(LRN). Whether they merge and explode, or whether they remain as a compact binary, depends on how soon the CE is ejected. If the CE isn't dissipated soon enough, the continued drag forces the stars closer together until they merge and erupt.

This simple graphic demonstrates how common envelopes evolve. At first, on star fills its Roche lobe. Then, the companion is engulfed and both stars orbit one another inside the common envelope. Then, either the common envelope is ejected and the stars remain as a binary, or the common envelope isn't ejected, and the stars are forced to merge. Image Credit: By Philip D. Hall - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/55287112.

According to recent reports, this is a coarse overview of the process. Astronomers know it can happen, and they'd like to learn more about it. But they need to observe them, and that's tough to do. Not only are they difficult to predict, but they're also relatively rare.

Observations with the JWST and other telescopes have found one CE situation where a main sequence star a little less massive than the Sun spiralled into its CE partner, a puffy supergiant star, and erupted as a LRN. This happened in our neighbouring galaxy, Andromeda. The observations and details are in newly introduced research in Nature titled "An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion." The first author is Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York.

"The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars," the authors write. "This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag.".

According to recent reports, that much is known by astrophysical theory. But nobody's observed the end of the inspiral and the eruption yet. "Here, we present observations of ATâ2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy," the researchers write.

Industry observers note that astronomers have lots of observations of ATâ2025abao with multiple telescopes because it's been experiencing brightness changes for several years and has attracted their attention. They've become familiar with ATâ2025abao and now simply refer to it as 'Bao'.

According to recent reports, âStellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict,â stated first author Karambelkar. âHowever, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the starsâ eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescopeâs data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.â.

According to recent reports, stars in these situations orbit each other for thousands of years with little change, and that was true of ATâ2025abao. But once they contacted each other, things changed. Other stars in CEs take thousands of orbits before they merge. But this one was different from other CE binaries. The pair merged after only 7 orbits (about 7 years.).

According to recent reports, observations go back as far as 2018, and between then and early 2025, the star gradually brightened in optical light. After that, it gradually faded in optical light, but its infrared light continued to brighten. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. It brightened by 100 times in the r-band over a period 25 days, and its temperature jumped to about 8000 Kelvin. Then, for about 80 days it plateaued and cooled down to about 3000 Kelvin. The JWST observed it during this period, only 47 days after its peak.

According to recent reports, âWe thought an outburst from a such an extended star would take years,â said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. âOne day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!â.

Recent findings suggest that âWhen a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect â a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Baoâs data,â stated co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Newly introduced York. âAs the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary starâs outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.â.

This was when the CEE began. The primary star engulfed the companion star in a common envelope, and drag stole its momentum, forcing it to spiral inward. This is when the JWST saw the destructive merger.

In a recent development, this is the finding chart for AT 2025abao. It was captured by the Asiago 67/92cm Schmidt telescope on 7 November 2025, when the light was at is maximum. M 31's (Andromeda) spiral disk is just visible on the left of the image. The zoomed-in panel indicates the transient. Image Credit: Reguitti et al. A&A, 709, A25 (2026).

It has been revealed that since the transient has been in the watchful eyes of astronomers for so long, they have detailed spectroscopy from it. The SPHEREx near-infrared space observatory played an vital role, catching the star in its survey. "In July 2025, the source was serendipitously observed during its rapid optical fading by the first sky survey of the SPHEREx mission, providing a precise glimpse of the stellar photosphere during this phase," the researchers state. That let them determine the masses of the stars, but only with some help from simulations.

As in a lot of astronomy research, simulations played an important role here. In this research, the authors worked with different models of CEE until the outcome of one matched the JWST's detailed observations of the star and its surrounding dust, shed by the primary star over hundreds of years.

It has been revealed that that work revealed that the primary was seven times more massive than the Sun, with a radius 350 times larger. It was also 18,000 times brighter than our star. âIt was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data,â said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

According to recent reports, the modelling also revealed the smaller star's true nature. It had only about 0.7 solar masses, one-tenth as massive as the other star. Its radius was much smaller and it was also much dimmer.

Industry observers note that the astronomers called the pair Big Bao and Little Bao, and when Little Bao was engulfed, there was a massive explosion. Only more observations will reveal what the resulting star, now simply called Bao, looks like.

It has been revealed that these artist's illustrations help explain what happened with ATâ2025abao and its common envelope evolution. The first panel shows the quiescent phase, when the stars are surrounded by a common envelope. The brightness was consistent during this phase. The second panel shows the stars brightening in the precursor stage. The companion star experiences drag and begins to spiral toward the primary star. In the third panel, there's a sudden bright eruption, as the companion spiralled and the common envelope is ejected. The JWST observed this. Then, in the final panel, months after the eruption, gas from the starâs ejected envelope freely expanded at the poles, but not at the equator, where previous ejecta from the more massive star was concentrated. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Leah Hustak (STScI); Science: Viraj Karambelkar (Columbia).

According to recent reports, "The 2025 eruption of ATâ2025abao displays the defining hallmarks of Luminous Red Novae, a class of transients established to arise from impulsive energy injection into a common envelope during the merger of a star with its companion," the authors write. But it's different from all other known LRN. It's progenitor is unambiguously an evolved AGB star with an extended convective envelope.

According to recent reports, "In contrast, all known LRN progenitors have primary stars on the main sequence," the researchers explain. But classical CEE theory claims that the primary star should be an AGB star.

"Thus, ATâ2025abao provides the first view of a classical CEE progenitor system continuously monitored from its onset through its culmination," the authors explain.

Watching a common envelope evolution in real time like this is a first in astronomy. Astronomers have had to perform a sort of forensic astrophysical study of transients like this in other cases, trying to reconstruct what happened thousands or even millions of years ago. Even with powerful telescopes and computer simulations, and with detailed theoretical frameworks to guide their work, that's tough to do.

Recent findings suggest that but this work opens a new window into CEE and how efficient it can be. And it's just in time to help with a potential flood of upcoming transient detections. Only a few dozen luminous red novae have been detected, but the Vera Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will detect hundreds of them, possibly thousands. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will also detect some LRN and CEE, but probably far fewer.

Recent findings suggest that this work lays the foundation for understanding some of what those surveys will find. In a few years time, astronomers should have a much clearer understanding of common envelope evolution and luminous red novae.

"This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys," the authors write.

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” notes Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago.

An industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in Upcoming York City.

In a recent development, something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago.

Recent findings suggest that an upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago.

According to recent reports, the gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City.

A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago.

In a recent development, gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago.

Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics company out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville.

Sources indicate that the pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in Fresh York City.

Fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago.

Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago.

It has been revealed that A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in Upcoming Orleans.

According to recent reports, the kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City.

A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia.

A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in Fresh York City.

It has been revealed that the perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). “Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone new at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver.

Many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives.

And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks.

A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia.

#111660. Scientists Catch Water Molecules Breaking Apart Before Their Electrons Can Respond

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (610 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists Catch Water Molecules Breaking Apart Before Their Electrons Can Respond

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When X-rays strike a water molecule, the molecule can break apart faster than its electrons can complete a fundamental relaxation process.
  • The discovery challenges established interpretations of how water responds to X-ray radiation.
  • When a water molecule absorbs a sufficiently energetic X-ray photon, an electron can be ejected from an inner shell of its oxygen atom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When X-rays strike a water molecule, the molecule can break apart faster than its electrons can complete a fundamental relaxation process. Scientists have discovered that both bonds holding hydrogen to oxygen can rupture within just a few femtoseconds, leaving behind an excited, electrically neutral oxygen atom.

The discovery challenges established interpretations of how water responds to X-ray radiation. It also identifies a previously overlooked source of highly reactive atomic oxygen, which can participate in further chemical reactions.

When a water molecule absorbs a sufficiently energetic X-ray photon, an electron can be ejected from an inner shell of its oxygen atom. The resulting vacancy normally triggers Auger decay, a rapid process in which another electron fills the vacancy and transfers enough energy to eject a second electron.

It has been revealed that however, the researchers found that the molecular structure can change even faster. The particular electronic state produced by X-ray absorption creates strong repulsive forces, allowing both oxygen-hydrogen bonds to break before Auger decay occurs.

“What makes this result particularly exciting is that we see the molecule break apart before the electronic relaxation has even finished. Both O–H bonds rupture within the lifetime of the oxygen core hole, so the nuclear motion is essentially winning the race against the electrons,” explained Florian Trinter of FHI in Berlin.

The team examined isolated water molecules in the gas phase using high-resolution electron spectroscopy at two synchrotron facilities: PETRA III at DESY in Hamburg, Germany, and the FlexPES beamline at MAX IV in Lund, Sweden.

Both experiments detected unusually sharp peaks at specific electron energies. These features could not be explained by the electronic decay of intact water molecules or the molecular fragments typically expected after X-ray absorption.

According to recent reports, “Seeing the characteristic signal also at MAX IV was an important part of establishing this as a genuine molecular fragmentation pathway. The measurements at the two facilities give us a very consistent picture of what happens to the water molecule after X-ray excitation,” mentioned Gunnar Öhrwall of MAX IV in Lund.

In a recent development, to determine what produced the unusual electron signals, the researchers performed detailed molecular and atomic calculations. The predicted electron energies matched the decay of excited neutral oxygen atoms rather than hydroxyl (OH) fragments.

In a recent development, this distinction matters because the energies of emitted electrons depend on the electronic structure of the atom or molecule producing them. The exceptionally narrow spectral features provided a recognizable signature of oxygen that had already separated from the original water molecule.

“The energy of the emitted electrons provides a kind of fingerprint of the state that is formed. Our calculations show that the observed features are consistent with the decay of an excited neutral oxygen atom that has already separated from the water molecule,” explained Ludger Inhester of CFEL at DESY in Hamburg.

The results offer a latest explanation for high-energy electron features observed in earlier water experiments. Signals previously associated with hydroxyl fragments may instead originate from excited neutral oxygen atoms produced through extremely rapid molecular fragmentation.

Because neutral atomic oxygen is highly reactive, understanding how it forms could improve models of chemical processes initiated by X-ray radiation. The findings also provide a more precise basis for interpreting electron spectra from water and related molecular systems.

Reference: “Ultrafast Dissociation of Water Producing Atomic Oxygen following Excitation above the O 1s Threshold” by Florian Trinter, Stephan Thürmer, Qi Zhou (周琪), Uwe Hergenhahn, Bernd Winter, Olle Björneholm, Maxim Tchaplyguine, Ludger Inhester and Gunnar Öhrwall, 5 November 2026, Physical Review Letters. DOI: 10.1103/c1hm-82p2.

Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona.
  • It has been revealed that the key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve stated before, is energy transfer.
  • It has been revealed that dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every week for the past few months weâve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sunâs surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a newly introduced paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as âdynamic fibrils.â They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sunâs outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

It has been revealed that the key to understanding this discrepancy, as weâve stated before, is energy transfer. How does the pathway work for energy to come from the Sunâs interior to its upper atmosphere? At this point, the accepted answer seems to be through massive magnetic fields pushing plasma outwards and heating it intensely, but the nuances of the exact mechanism remain hazy.

It has been revealed that dynamic fibrils are one such potential mechanism. They are rhythmic jets erupting from the outer haloâknown as the penumbraâsurrounding a sunspot. But up until now we have had difficulty tracking where exactly they go, largely because the Sun is so bright it's hard to isolate individual tendrils from the overall burning mass of plasma.

Fraser attempts to answer why the Sun's corona is hotter than its surface.

Industry observers note that to do so, Guotang Wu and Xiaoli Yan of the Yunnan Observatories at the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined data sources. They used the Latest Vacuum Solar Telescope, located in southwestern China, to monitor a sunspot in an active region of the Sun known as NOAA 13182. Crucially, they did so for just over an hour on January 10th, 2023, and took snapshots of the chromosphere â the middle layer between the Sunâs surface and its outer atmosphere â every 45 seconds. They then combined these ground observations with data from Chinaâs CHASE solar satellite and NASAâs Solar Dynamics Observatory, providing a multi-layered and multi-spectral view of this active sunspot.

Over that hour of observations, they catalogued 176 individual dynamic fibrils â jets of plasma that rise off the surface and into the Sunâs atmosphere. On average, they do so at a speed of 16 km/s, faster than the speed of sound in the surrounding plasma medium of the chromosphere. But eventually they slow down, falling back to the surface after an average lifespan of about 4.5 minutes. Even during that time, they manage to stretch on average 1,130 kilometers â roughly the distance from New York to Chicago.

So where do those jets come from in the first place? Sunspots are already famous for creating features known as ârunning penumbral wavesâ of compressed gas that move across the halo surrounding the sunspotâs core. According to math described in the paper, the rhythmic pulsing of the fibrils almost matches the five-minute cadence of the running penumbral waves in the sunspot. This, in turn, points to another underlying phenomena â magnetoacoustic waves.

Fraser talks about the highest resolution image ever taken of the Sun.

Under the surface of the Sun, hot convection cells of plasma constantly vibrate features known as âmagnetic flux tubesâ, creating low-frequency sound waves that leak upwards into the chromosphere. As the gas they are traversing gets thinner and thinner, they grow steeper and stronger until they âbreakâ in a similar manner to waves on a beach. However, these breaking waves are not like those of water â each breaking wave is accompanied by a miniature sonic boom known as a magnetoacoustic shock. These push the plasma residing in the chromosphere where they break, pushing chromospheric plasma upward to form dynamic fibrils.

Buried in the data there was a clear pattern of how much the orientation of these magnetic fields matters for the creation of fibrils. When the magnetic field lines point straight up, the plasma jets experience stronger deceleration and pulse at shorter intervals. Whereas when the fields lean more horizontally across the Sunâs surface, the fibrils decelerate more gently and pulse over longer periods. This confirmed a long-standing theory about how magnetic tilt affects solar sound waves.

To tie all this back to the original theme â extreme coronal heating â observations from SDO revealed corresponding signatures in gas heated to hundreds of thousands or even millions of degrees. So, the plasma pushed up by those shockwaves doesnât just appear to fizzle out - it directly transfers energy into the corona itself, which aligns with what many of the recent papers on this topic have been proving in various ways.

In a recent development, but weâre still not 100% sure of some of the nuances of how this complex magnetic dance actually works. That might have to wait for even bigger ground-based telescopes such as the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, which can resolve the magnetic threads inside these massive jets. But until then, we have an even clearer picture of how an acoustic hum plays a role in stoking the inferno of the Sunâs outer atmosphere.

Latest Update: As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As Democrats continue their victory lap after their major wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their major wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

Recent findings suggest that for Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”.

“The most vital lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

In a recent development, voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer remarked.

He acknowledged, however, that their prepares could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer noted, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the fresh session.”.

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

In a recent development, the group isn’t alone in floating a latest approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

According to recent reports, sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”.

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”.

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”.

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a upcoming precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who stated he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

It has been revealed that and Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how key the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

Industry observers note that none of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

In a recent development, the next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”.

Sources indicate that “For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he remarked, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”.

Recent findings suggest that even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the newly introduced Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”.

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”.

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”.

It has been revealed that but it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

Sources indicate that GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of Latest Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”.

According to recent reports, “The NDAA is such an vital bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he mentioned.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

According to recent reports, if you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Sources indicate that A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the fresh treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

In a recent development, you can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

It has been revealed that even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s latest holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

According to recent reports, when it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

In a recent development, it really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

Industry observers note that when it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

It has been revealed that those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

According to recent reports, is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

Industry observers note that we all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.
